```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
has_ffmpeg <- nzchar(Sys.which("ffmpeg"))
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

`whatsappaudioR` converts compressed mobile voice notes (the `.opus`/`.ogg`
files produced by WhatsApp and similar messaging apps) directly into tidy
data frames ready for analysis. This vignette walks through the core path:
**voice note -> tidy spectrogram -> plot -> features**.

## Reading a voice note

With your own file, reading a voice note is one line:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(whatsappaudioR)
w <- wa_read("voice_note.opus")
```

`wa_read()` detects the file extension and, for compressed formats, decodes
via a system `ffmpeg` binary into a `tuneR::Wave` object: the same
representation you'd get from `tuneR::readWave()` on a plain `.wav` file, so
the rest of the R audio ecosystem (`tuneR`, `seewave`) works on it unchanged.

The package ships a three-second example voice note, which the rest of this
vignette uses. Here it is decoded and resampled to 16 kHz mono:

```{r}
library(whatsappaudioR)

f <- system.file("extdata", "sample.opus", package = "whatsappaudioR")
if (has_ffmpeg) {
  w <- wa_read(f, sample_rate = 16000, mono = TRUE)
} else {
  # No FFmpeg on the machine that built this vignette: fall back to a
  # synthetic one-second 440 Hz tone so the remaining steps still run.
  w <- tuneR::sine(440, duration = 16000, samp.rate = 16000)
}
w
```

## Tidy spectrogram

```{r}
spec_df <- wa_spectrogram(w, wl = 1024)
head(spec_df)
```

`freq` is in kHz (matching `seewave`'s convention) and `amplitude` is in dB.
Because the result is a long-format tibble, it plots directly with
`ggplot2`:

```{r, eval = has_ggplot2}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(spec_df, aes(x = time, y = freq, fill = amplitude)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Frequency (kHz)", fill = "Amplitude (dB)")
```

## Spectral and temporal features

```{r}
feats <- wa_features(w)
dim(feats)
feats[, c("peak_freq_hz", "spectral_centroid_hz", "spectral_flatness",
          "pulse_rate_hz", "duty_cycle")]
```

Returns a one-row tibble of documented features: peak frequency, spectral
centroid, flatness, entropy, rolloff, dominant-frequency stability, a
harmonic-energy heuristic, temporal features computed from the amplitude
envelope, and 12 MFCCs. See `?wa_features` for exact definitions. Nothing
here is a black box: every column is a named, inspectable, conventional
bioacoustic or audio feature.

## Simulating compression

If you have clean, uncompressed audio and want to know how it would sound
(and measure) after passing through a WhatsApp-style pipeline:

```{r, eval = has_ffmpeg}
clean <- tuneR::sine(440, duration = 44100, samp.rate = 44100,
                     bit = 16, pcm = TRUE)
degraded <- wa_simulate_compression(clean, bitrate = 16000, sr = 16000)
degraded
```

This requires a system `ffmpeg` build with `libopus` support.

## Batch processing

```{r, eval = FALSE}
features_df <- wa_batch("voice_notes/", wa_features)
```

Applies any function of a `Wave` object (default `wa_features()`) across
every supported audio file in a directory, returning one row per file with
a `file` column.
